entries.note: Existed as an academic title before it meant a medical practitioner, from a root meaning to teach; the old English word for a doctor was [[see:leech]].
Old English word for a doctor, meaning healer or enchanter; the bloodsucking leeches may be named after doctors, or come from another source that merged with it.
An earlier, and still current, word for a doctor, from a root meaning nature; medieval physicians diagnosed illness, prescribed drugs and usually had university training.
Literally climb onto a bench, a seller of snake oils and remedies who performed from a bench in public marketplaces.
Its red wrapping supposedly represents a bloody bandage on the arm of someone bled at the [[see:barber]], who did bloodletting and dentistry.
Simply means bearder, from a Latin word for beard; people want it linked to [[unrelated:barbarian]], but it isn't.
Literally someone who works with their hands, its ending coming from Greek [[from:ergon]], work, also seen in [[same-root:synergy]] and [[same-root:ergonomic]].
Means working together, another word containing the Greek for work found in [[same-root:surgeon]].
From Greek for work: ergonomics is the study of how people work, so ergonomic products suit how people operate, not just the human form.
British surgeons are titled Mister rather than Doctor, a relic of surgery's low standing that is now worn almost as a badge of honour.
A 17th-century word for a surgeon; the form is unclear in the captions.
A grim 17th-century term for a surgeon.
An old insulting word for doctors and surgeons; the nim may be from Old English [[from?:niman]], to take, with gimmer added for bounce.
A 16th-century word for a surgeon, meaning someone who scratches at things; possibly related to [[same-root?:scar]].
A fraudulent or unqualified medical practitioner since the 17th century, a shortening of [[from:quacksalver]].
From a Middle Dutch element meaning to brag or boast plus salve: someone who boasts about their ointments; shortened to [[gave:quack]].
Germanic in origin and possibly simply meaning dry, from phrases for dry barrels used of shipped spices, herbs and medicines; it means both medicine and intoxicant.
An etymological doublet of [[same-root:poison]]; a potion could be a benevolent poison, reflecting how cures and poisons share names.
A doublet of [[same-root:potion]]; today poison is taken by mouth, unlike [[see:venom]], which goes under the skin.
Once meant medicine, drug or ointment as well as something harmful; now it is injected under the skin, unlike [[see:poison]].
From a Greek root that could mean a preparer of drugs or a poisoner, covering medicine, poison, charm and enchantment.
Means from cows, as smallpox was prevented with a small dose of [[from:cowpox]]; credited to [[see:Edward Jenner]], though [[see:Benjamin Jesty]] and others tried it earlier.
Credited with developing the [[see:vaccine]], though others experimented with the idea before him.
One of those who tried the [[see:vaccine]] idea before Jenner, inoculating his own family.
To inoculate originally meant to implant a bud into another plant, later extended to vaccines.
Scratching material from smallpox sores into the arm, risky as it could cause a bad case; from [[from:variola]].
Another word for smallpox, meaning speckled or spotted; gave [[gave:variolation]].
Greek-derived, meaning to burn or shine; the fifth element filling space, then a light colourless compound used as an anaesthetic in the 1840s.
A hypothetical medium thought to carry light through space, abandoned after an 1887 optics experiment found no ether wind; see [[see:ether]].
Latin for I will please; earlier the name of a funeral rite, from the chant Placebo Domino in regione vivorum; compare [[see:dirige]] and [[see:nocebo effect]].
A funeral rite named after the first word of its psalm, Dirige Domine, direct me O Lord; it gave [[gave:dirge]].
A corruption of [[from:dirige]], paralleling how [[see:placebo]] also came from the first word of a funeral psalm.
A directable balloon, discussed before, from the same root as [[same-root:dirige]].
Shares its root with [[same-root:dirige]] and [[same-root:dirigible]].
When negative expectations worsen outcomes; dates from about 1961, not a blend but Latin for I will harm, from [[from:nocere]]; the opposite of [[see:placebo]].
From a Greek root meaning numbness, deadness or stupor; shortened to [[gave:narc]].
A police informer, recorded in the 1800s and thought to come from a Romani word for nose; not ultimately related to [[unrelated:narc]], though influenced by it.
Short for narcotics agent, from [[from:narcotic]]; its usage almost certainly influenced the unrelated [[unrelated:nark]], informer.
Entered English around 1600, either from Latin laudare, to praise, or a Greek term for gum resin; coined by [[see:Paracelsus]] for a medicine containing opium.
Swiss figure called the father of toxicology, full name Philippus Aureolus Theophrastus Bombastus von Hohenheim, who coined [[see:laudanum]].
Basically means plant juice, specifically poppy juice; gave [[gave:opioid]].
Opium plus -oid, opium-like; the hosts debate whether opium itself is an opioid, as -oid suggests resembling rather than being, like [[see:asteroid]].
Star-shaped but not a star, an example of -oid meaning like the thing, compared with [[see:opioid]].
Human-shaped, whether human or not, another -oid example alongside [[see:opioid]].
Often taken as a cute little fact but meant as something not quite a fact, another -oid example alongside [[see:opioid]].
Named after [[from:Morpheus]], the Greek god of dreams; its chemical ending was echoed in [[see:heroin]] and [[see:cocaine]].
The Greek god of dreams, who came up in the Greek mythology episode, and who gave his name to [[gave:morphine]].
Coined by [[see:Bayer]] from the Greek root of hero, almost certainly blending [[from:heroine]] and [[from:morphine]]: a drug that heroically rescues you from pain.
The female hero, whose feminine ending differs from the chemical ending of [[see:heroin]], though the drug name puns on it.
Friedrich Bayer & Company, predecessor of the modern pharma giant, coined [[see:heroin]].
From coca leaves chewed for energy in the Andes, isolated in 1855; its ending echoes [[see:morphine]]; the DEA lists almost 500 street names for it.
Early Coca-Cola contained [[from:cocaine]] and was named after it, perhaps created as a [[see:coca wine]] without the wine.
A popular wine and patent medicine containing coca, notably [[see:Mariani wine]].
A [[see:coca wine]] created in the 1860s by [[see:Angelo Mariani]], a French chemist from Corsica.
One of the obvious, familiar street names for [[see:cocaine]] on the DEA list.
A familiar street name for [[see:cocaine]] on the DEA list.
A familiar street name for [[see:cocaine]] on the DEA list.
An obscure street name for [[see:cocaine]] that baffles the hosts.
An obscure street name for [[see:cocaine]] on the DEA list.
An obscure street name for [[see:cocaine]] on the DEA list.
Coined in 1956 by [[see:Humphry Osmond]], meaning to reveal in the mind; first used in a letter to [[see:Aldous Huxley]].
Canadian psychiatrist who experimented with mescaline and LSD, coined [[see:psychedelic]], and gave [[see:Aldous Huxley]] mescaline.
Author of Brave New World, recipient of the letter first using [[see:psychedelic]]; took mescaline under Osmond's observation, inspiring [[see:The Doors of Perception]].
Book [[see:Aldous Huxley]] wrote based on his mescaline experience supervised by [[see:Humphry Osmond]].
A real condition of hearing loud noises in your sleep, which Jess correctly identified in an earlier quiz.
When the body cannot break down a compound found in some foods, making you smell of fish.
Fainting at the sight of something beautiful, named after [[from:Stendhal]], who felt ill amid Florence's art and tombs.
Pen name of French author Marie-Henri Beyle, who described palpitations and faintness in Florence, giving [[gave:Stendhal syndrome]].
Also called [[see:Cotard's syndrome]], the delusion that you are dead; about half of patients think they never existed, the rest that they are immortal.
The other name for [[see:walking corpse syndrome]].
Gut fungi ferment carbohydrates into alcohol, so people can feel drunk or hungover without drinking.
Brain damage from a stroke or trauma can leave someone speaking with a different accent, which Rob finds incomprehensible.
A silly historical ailment supposedly afflicting women who rode bicycles, making their faces uglier.
Literally things that happen at the same time, implying no cause and effect.
Ends in Greek gnosis, knowing; means to tell two things apart.
From Greek gnosis, knowing: to know something in advance; [[see:prognostication]] was an earlier word for it.
Shares the knowing root of [[same-root:prognosis]].
An earlier word for [[see:prognosis]].
Italian for influence, originally any epidemic, blamed on the influence of the stars; flu is unrelated to flowing.
Referred to as one of the hosts' favourite etymologies from earlier discussions, compared with [[see:influenza]].
Once any wasting disease, something that consumes you, later the older word for [[see:tuberculosis]].
Not about tubes but tubers, swellings and lumps, referring to the lymph nodes.
Plural of mump, a 1580s verb meaning to whine or mutter like a beggar, from Dutch for cheat; also meant a fit of sullenness.
Just means spots or blemishes; Middle English measel was an adjective meaning leprous.
From French for a drop, as it was thought viscous humours dripped into the joints, per [[see:humorism]]; compare [[see:dropsy]].
The theory of bodily juices, discussed before, behind the naming of [[see:gout]].
A morbid accumulation of watery liquid in the body, a notion similar to [[see:gout]].
Related to [[same-root:rage]], both from Latin rabere, to be mad; also called [[see:hydrophobia]], [[see:aerophobia]] and [[see:pantophobia]].
Shares its Latin origin, to be mad or rave, with [[same-root:rabies]].
An older name for [[see:rabies]], since sufferers sometimes cannot make themselves drink water.
Dread of air, an old name for [[see:rabies]] because it makes breathing hard.
Fear of all things, an old name for [[see:rabies]] because sufferers become generally paranoid.
Means flowing seed, from the flowing root shared with [[same-root:rhythm]]; also called [[see:the clap]].
Means flowing through, from the root shared with [[same-root:rhythm]].
Means flowing blood, from the root shared with [[same-root:rhythm]].
Means general drippy discharge, from the flowing root shared with [[same-root:rhythm]].
A beautiful word from the same flowing root as [[same-root:gonorrhea]] and [[same-root:diarrhea]].
Name for [[see:gonorrhea]] from French clapier bubo, a groin swelling caught by visiting a [[from:clapier]].
Literally a rabbit's nest or warren, a euphemism for a brothel, which gave [[gave:the clap]].
From a Greek root meaning a mantle or military cloak, because it cloaks the nucleus of an infected cell.
Borrowed from Greek, meaning creeping; in Greek it meant shingles, now [[see:herpes zoster]]; used for many skin conditions, even in oysters.
Today's name for shingles, zoster being Greek for belt or girdle from where the disease commonly appears; see [[see:herpes]].
Named after the shepherd Syphilis in the 1530 poem [[from:Syphilis, or the French Disease]]; the name may mean pig lover.
A 1530 poem in which the sun punishes a shepherd for cursing it by unleashing the disease, giving [[gave:syphilis]] its name.
Name for [[see:syphilis]] across Europe, from [[from:Syphilis, or the French Disease]] and French soldiers catching it in Italy; compare [[equivalent:the Italian disease]].
What the French called [[see:syphilis]], fairly, since that was where it was picked up; compare [[equivalent:the French disease]].
The German term for the cervix, an example of German using literal descriptions that medical Greek and Latin disguise.
From Latin [[from:hospitalis]], a place welcoming guests, first lodging pilgrims and travellers; [[same-root:hotel]] and [[same-root:hostel]] are clipped versions.
A clipped version of the same Latin word as [[same-root:hospital]].
A clipped version of the same Latin word as [[same-root:hospital]].
An order set up in Jerusalem during the Crusades to lodge poor pilgrims, later protecting them, fighting and governing Rhodes and Malta.
The cross of the [[see:Knights Hospitaller]], who ruled Malta, yet it is not the cross on the [[see:flag of Malta]].
Red and white bars with the [[see:George Cross]] in the top corner, not the [[see:Maltese cross]].
Medal awarded to Malta by the king in the Second World War, shown on the [[see:flag of Malta]].
Taken from French during the Revolutionary Wars, when ambulances were field hospitals; literally a walking hospital, unlike German [[equivalent:Krankenwagen]].
The German for [[equivalent:ambulance]], literally a sick car, which Rob thinks better conveys urgency.
From Greek klinike techne, bedside or sickbed practice: where you lie down to be examined; related to [[same-root:incline]] and [[same-root:lean]].
One of the leaning words related to [[same-root:clinic]].
Related to [[same-root:clinic]].
Originally part of a Greek phrase with techne, the art of something, like [[see:clinic]].
Originally from a Greek phrase with techne, like [[see:clinic]].
Gyn means woman, so it is the department dealing with women.
Literally to stand opposite, from Latin [[from:obstetrix]], the woman standing opposite one giving birth; semantically parallel to [[see:midwife]].
The person who stands with the woman giving birth, a genuine semantic parallel to [[see:obstetrics]].
Ortho, right or correct, plus pedics, children, like [[same-root:pediatrics]]: originally correcting children's conditions like rickets and polio.
Shares the children element of [[same-root:orthopedics]].
Contains ortho, right or correct; orthography is writing correctly, illustrating [[same-root:orthopedics]].
Of the right opinion, dox meaning opinion; more judgmental than conventional, covered in Rob's newsletter.
The study of disease or suffering; pathologists seek what caused death, but many, like speech pathologists, never deal with dead people.
The healing of the soul or psyche, contrasted with [[see:neurology]].
The study of the neurons or nerves, more broadly the brain, contrasted with [[see:psychiatry]].
